Descriptive.question: You had to go on a train journey with your family. On reaching the railway station, you discovered your train was delayed by two hours. You have recently visited a government hospital. Describe the sights and sounds which upset you. What would you like to do to change the situation for the better if you were the Health minister of your state?

You have recently shifted to a new city. Describe the area where you live, your next-door neighbours, the difficulties you faced while shifting and why you like / dislike the place.
Give a vivid description of a popular wayside restaurant and account for its popularity.

Last year, you visited your grandparents. There, you participated in a local festival. Describe the way people were dressed, the different cultural events, and the food sold in the stalls. What were your feelings as you returned from the festivities?
It is the first time that you went to a beach. Describe the sights and the sounds and all the activity that you saw during the time you were there.

You travel to school in an autorickshaw every day with two other students. Describe the auto driver and the experience of travelling in the auto. Give details of the familiar sights and sounds you see daily.

Imagine that you visited a remote village untouched by the influence of technology. Describe the village, the people, their routine and at least one person you met there. How did you feel at first? What were your feelings when you had to return?

One of your classmates is leaving school because his or her father has been transferred. He or she has been very popular with everyone while she was at the school. Describe in detail a touching farewell that you have planned for him/her. Give a vivid description of the preparation and the feelings of all the friends and teachers.

Your neighbour requested you to help her son who is in Class 5 with his studies. Narrate your experience of tutoring him and the impact it had on you.

You had gone on a day trip with your friends to a place located on the outskirts of the city. A few hours before your return, the roads were closed because of torrential rain. Narrate your experience of being stranded in a remote place and how you and your friends overcame the challenging circumstances.

Imagine a situation where your car developed trouble on the road. There was no option but to push it to the nearest mechanic shop for repair. Explain what you did and what you learnt from the experience.

Argumentative.question: All school examinations should be open-book. Express your views either FOR or AGAINST the given statement.
Parents should discuss money issues with their children. Argue either FOR or AGAINST.
Mobile phones are our enemies and not friends. Express your views either FOR or AGAINST the given statement.
Exams should not be part of the schooling system. Express your views either FOR or AGAINST.
Films should be made to escape from reality, not to show how grim life is. Argue either FOR or AGAINST this idea.
Parents should not influence their children when choosing the subjects they wish to study. Argue either FOR or AGAINST the given statement.
A foreign language should be made compulsory in school curriculum. Express your views either FOR or AGAINST.
Argumentative.answer:
Imagine you go to France or Spain and you are completely unfamiliar with the French or Spanish language. How would you handle an environment that makes you feel like you cannot read or write? The situation is challenging, to say the least. With the world becoming an interconnected global village, mastery over or at least a basic understanding of a foreign language is an essential skillset. Hence, it is important to add a foreign language in the school curriculum. With this thought in mind, the Greater Chennai Corporation now plans to teach French as an additional language to Class 11 students.
Canadian psycholinguist Frank Smith said, “Language is not a genetic gift, it is a social gift. Learning a new language is becoming a member of the club—the community of speakers of that language.”
Fluency in a language grants access to a comfort zone that can be beneficial for making friends, securing contracts and nurturing relationships. It will be a significant asset in the job market. Employers also seek candidates who can communicate with international clients, understand global markets, and navigate cross-cultural negotiations. Bilingual or multilingual employees will have an advantage in fields like diplomacy, tourism and international relations.
By making foreign language education compulsory, schools can help Indian students have a competitive advantage over people from other countries.
Additionally, research has shown that acquiring a second language can enhance brain function, problem-solving abilities and creativity. Bilingual individuals often exhibit better memory retention, heightened attention span and superior multitasking abilities compared to monolingual individuals. This cognitive flexibility is not only beneficial academically but also in everyday life, where adaptability and quick thinking are irreplaceable.
Additional language classes in the school curriculum are advisable because children have a remarkable ability to absorb new languages than adults. Early exposure to a foreign language significantly improves fluency. Early proficiency can also pave the way for advanced language study in higher education and seamless integration into multilingual work environments.
As our world becomes increasingly polarised, learning a foreign language can promote understanding and empathy among citizens, enhancing relationships in multicultural societies. The ability to communicate in another language would give opportunities to explore different cultures, traditions and perspectives. It would inspire young children to see the world from a wider perspective and value the diversity that defines our global society. This cultural awareness is crucial in combating stereotypes, reducing prejudice, and promoting tolerance and mutual respect among people of different backgrounds. If the Indian Premier League can bridge barriers in cricketing terms, language can do the same between citizens.
A Czech proverb says “Learn a new language and get a new soul.” It is time for us to ensure our students pour their heart into learning a new language.

Argumentative.question: The expression of personal details on social media has eroded the right to privacy. Express if you agree or disagree with the statement.
'The best things in life come free'. Write either FOR or AGAINST the statement.
Argumentative.answer:
‘The best things in life come free’. Write either FOR or AGAINST the statement.
Who does not like a free product? That is why most people rush to buy a product if the deal is combined with a freebie. Often, we fail to recognise that there is no such thing as a free lunch, as economist Milton Friedman emphasised. There is usually a hidden cost when something is offered for free. Hence, I believe that the best things in life do not come free.
For example, free electricity, free water, free bus travel for women which are provided by different state governments in India. While they appear to be given freely to the individual, they are funded through taxes. The cruel irony lies in the fact that these citizens have to allocate more of their income towards taxes for road usage or fuel in order to support this free service. The government gives with one hand and takes back with the other.
Nowadays, if you are not the one paying, you become the product. Online platforms entice you by offering a giveaway only to collect data, such as user behaviour. This data is utilised for target advertising and pushes the consumer to buy products.
When we think about abstract elements of life such as love and friendship, it may appear that these emotions are priceless. However, there is a cost to bear even for these 'best' things. Unless you invest time, effort, emotions, sacrifice or even material resources, even love and friendship are not achievable.
Let us take the example of the commitment required to raise a child. While the love of the little one is priceless, it will be returned if you spend quality time with the child and take care of his or her needs. The same goes with pets. Dogs do not judge you based on your wealth, but they do show affection by wagging their tails if you take care of their hunger and emotional need. Time holds value just like money, so the notion of 'free' should not solely be measured in currency.
One may experience extreme sense of joy after getting a promotion at work. However, this often meant sacrificing family and personal well-being. Making this moment happen also required years of education, training, and hard work as additional investments.
Hence, believing that 'the best things in life come free' is a myth that distorts the complex maze of life. The best things in life are certainly valuable, but it would be wrong to assume that they happen at zero cost.

Argumentative.question: The well-being of a society is enhanced when many of its people question those in authority. Argue either FOR or AGAINST.
Argumentative.answer:
The well-being of a society is enhanced when many of its people question those in authority. Argue either FOR or AGAINST.
Imagine the outcome, if there had not been widespread outrage in India following the gang-rape of Nirbhaya in Delhi in 2012 or a similar crime against a veterinary doctor in Hyderabad in 2019. It would have been impossible for us to convince our lawmakers to make stronger laws against atrocities against women. I believe the well-being of a society is improved when most people ask for accountability from those in authority.
A society on the ‘Mute’ button is as good as dead. A society that questions authority is the only one that thrives. This questioning compels accountability and a more just society. This could mean a group of farmers questioning how certain farm laws were planned. In an academic world, college students may confront the principal over decisions they think as limiting their freedom to express themselves.
Furthermore, questioning authority is necessary because no one is perfect. It gives those in positions of power the ability to see things from a fresh angle and implement necessary corrections. Moreover, history has several examples of unchecked power leading to oppression and injustice. The act of questioning those in authority has been vital in dismantling autocratic systems, whether it be tyrannical monarchs or corrupt officials. When you start asking questions, it may seem like a David versus Goliath battle because the authorities appear unbeatable. However, both the Indian Independence movement and the anti-apartheid movement in South Africa were characterised by the use of public defiant and questioning of discriminatory laws, which ultimately brought about positive change.
Hence, when citizens are encouraged to critically analyse the status quo, ask questions, and propose alternative solutions, it leads to a lively environment where new ideas can flourish. Scientific progress, often stems from challenging established theories and seeking new explanations. For example, it was Copernicus who defied authority to state that the sun, and not the earth, is at the centre of the Universe.
However, questioning does not mean disrespect. A healthy questioning attitude involves critical thinking, fact-based arguments, and a willingness to find solutions. It is about holding authorities accountable for their decisions while recognising the need for order and effective leadership. Increased public scrutiny promotes greater transparency in decision-making. There is no better example than the election process in a democracy, where the citizen questions authority and its decisions by either voting out the party in power or re-electing it with a wafer-thin majority.

Expository.question: Photographs
Expository.answer:
The creation of a photograph is a work of physics with the interplay of light, shadows, and colours creating magic. However, at a philosophical level, it is unquestionably a masterpiece. When you consider the added element of preserving precious memories forever, it transforms any piece to the highest form of literature. In a nutshell, they are a window to the past, exquisite expressions of artistic vision and a handy tool for documentation of a moment. Photographs are stories without words.
A time machine has always been an object of fancy for many and a trend for science fiction writers. Photographs are nothing less than a time machine with the ability to transport anyone to another time in an instant, stirring our mind with memories, both happy and sad. That is perhaps why pre-wedding photo shoots, maternity photo shoots and even divorce party photo shoots have become a trend. The idea is to capture that moment so that it is possible to return to them to relive that occasion in the mind forever and share those stories.
In the broader context of a society and a nation, photographs of significant historical events or renowned figures become part of our shared heritage, influencing our perspective on history and shaping our identity. Celebrated photojournalists like Raghu Rai, India’s first woman photojournalist Homai Vyarawalla and Pulitzer Prize winner Danish Siddiqui have deeply influenced the way we see the India in the past and the present.
Beyond documentation and memory, photography is also a powerful medium of artistic expression. Photographers use light, composition and perspective to convey emotions, narratives and abstract concepts. The digital cameras have now democratised the world of photography, allowing anyone to capture images. Photographs are now an integral part of the craft of storytelling and the way we interact in the online space.
However, technology comes with a downside too. In a world filled with paparazzi and intrusive cameras, personal privacy becomes a casualty. The ability to edit images has meant what you see is often not what it is. Digital images are altered and manipulated, whether it is done innocently with the intention of enhancing their appearance on social media platforms like Instagram or Facebook. Some people do it with the purpose of avoiding negative feedback or intentionally misrepresenting oneself to tarnish the other person’s reputations. In the dark world of fake images, ethics have become outdated.
Photographs can now be taken without pressing a button. In the world of AI, apps can create almost real images, rendering the eyes and mind of a photographer obsolete. Take a moment to think about the photo studio photographer waiting in vain for anyone wanting family portraits or passport-sized photos. This trade is now a thing of the past, with its obituary already written.

Expository.question: Greed
Expository.answer:
Greed is described as a selfish yearning for something that should not be yours. It is used particularly in the context of wealth, power or food, where individuals or groups crave for more. It is so often seen that the corrupt and the gluttonous engage in unethical practices to increase their profits or acquire an advantage.
Leo Tolstoy’s famous story ‘How much land does a man need?’ is the best example to show that greed invariably meets a tragic end. In the story, a peasant is promised that all the land he walks on and returns to the starting point by sunset will be his. The man keeps running in his quest to cover as much as possible, but by the time he gets back, he is so exhausted that he collapses and dies. Finally, all he needed for his grave was six feet of land.
Greed is an overwhelmingly negative emotion, as it knows no bounds. A raid by the Anti-Corruption Bureau at the house of a revenue superintendent in Nizamabad district of Telangana in August 2024 unearthed six crore rupees in cash, jewellery and properties. The wealth was disproportionate to known sources of income for this government servant and had obviously come through dubious means. Undoubtedly, greed operates in a similar manner to addiction. If a person is addicted, the desire to accumulate more through dishonest methods does not have a limit.
The same goes with food where the urge to eat without control has severe side effects on one’s health. As people get older, the inability to control their eating becomes evident in the diagnostic lab reports that point to health complications. Similarly, even young people have a desire for junk food, which leads to obesity.
At a metaphorical level, greed represents the darker side of human nature that leads to the corruption of the soul. William Shakespeare essays it in ‘Macbeth’ where the protagonist, driven by greed and ambition, goes down on the path of self-destruction. Likewise, the story of King Midas, who turned everything he touched into gold, is a classic example of how greed can be both a gift and a curse.
Does excessive greed always show moral corruption? An exception could be when the leader of a country or a state wants more rewards for the people of his region and bargains hard for the same. Such focus on self-interest can also be beneficial, as it could further drive economic growth and development.
The only way the negativity of greed can be rid of is by teaching the right moral values from childhood and by identifying any signs of insecurities that a child may suffer from. If the root causes can be addressed, it can be drilled into the young mind that greed comes with a one-way ticket to hell.
